To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the median dominates the average of closest two observations for normal and uniform distributions, but the latter dominates the former for Cauchy and double–exponential distributions.

(1) the median is superior to the average of the closest two measurements for a broad class (including normal, Cauchy and uniform) of distributions and for a broad classof loss functions, (2) the mean of the two closest measurements can have smaller risk than the sample median for some contamination models and loss functions and (3) the average of the most concordant two measurements is a robust location estimator for the uniform distribution.

the median dominates the average of two closest observations for normal, uniform, double–exponetial and Cauchy distributions and the average of two closes observations can dominate the median under a particular contamination model and loss function.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the estimation of a parameter $\mu$, when the observations $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$ are independent, identically distributed, and the density of $X_i$ is symmetric about the unknown parameter $\mu$. The estimator of interest is the sample median, $\hat\mu_1$, which is the midmost observation.
the estimation of a parameter $\theta $ in the case where the observations are contaminated by a small proportion of gross errors.
the problem of estimating location in samples of three.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for the loss functions considered the median is the better estimator in the sense of stochastic dominance.
, for most practical purposes, the sample median is the best estimator of location for samples of size three, but that the average of the closest two is a better estimator in certain situations.
the median is a more robust estimator of location in samples from symmetric distributions than the average of the closest two.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the median is a better estimator than the average of the closest two for most practical purposes.
the median is a good resistant estimator in many cases but is not always superior.

, for the loss functions considered, the average of the closest two measurements is the superior resistant estimate for a uniform population, the median is the superior resistant estimators for normal and double–exponential populations and the average of the most concordant two observations is the superior resistant estimates for a Cauchy population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for the loss functions considered here, the median is the superior robust estimator in a large number of cases.
the median is a more robust estimator for a broad range of distributions, but that the mean of the two closest values may be preferable in some contamination models.
the median is a robust estimator of location, but that there are cases in which other robust estimators are better.
